euwallacea-similis.summary: This slender, light-brown ambrosia beetle is a wood inhabitant with a broad range of host trees. Its narrow shape and the small bumps on the sloping rear of its wing covers help specialists separate it from similar beetles. Records often use the older name Xyleborus similis, so tracking those names matters when comparing reports of this introduced species.

sources.label: Netherlands NPPO: Euwallacea similis risk scan
University of Florida and US Forest Service: North American Xyleborini

syngonium-podophyllum.summary: Familiar as an indoor arrowhead plant, American evergreen becomes a vigorous climbing vine in warm, shaded landscapes. Young leaves have the recognizable arrow shape, while established plants can spread across the ground and climb trees. In Florida natural areas, dense growth can suppress native vegetation and add weight to branches. Discarded garden material is one route by which this ornamental escapes cultivation.

caprella-scaura.summary: Caprella scaura is a small marine amphipod that grips seaweeds, branching animals, and submerged structures. Females brood their young, which initially cling to their mother. Dense introduced populations can crowd other small crustaceans. Its original home remains uncertain, and several similar forms have been grouped under this name, complicating the story of its worldwide spread.

phellodendron-amurense.summary: Amur corktree takes its name from its soft, deeply furrowed bark. This spreading deciduous tree bears opposite leaves divided into several leaflets, with a strong resinous scent when crushed. Female trees produce clusters of small fruits that turn black. Introduced as a landscape tree from eastern Asia, it can seed beyond cultivation, and the University of Connecticut documents an invasive tendency in that state.

sources.label: University of Connecticut Plant Database: Amur corktree

rhinogobius-brunneus.summary: The Amur goby is a small bottom-dwelling fish with joined pelvic fins that form a suction-cup-like disc. Breeding males can show striking red or blue colors and pale fin edges. USGS records fish under this name from the Columbia River region, but cautions that Rhinogobius brunneus has been used for a complex of similar species. That uncertainty matters when interpreting its life history and introduced range.

sources.label: USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species: Amur goby

lonicera-maackii.summary: Amur honeysuckle is a large deciduous shrub with opposite, pointed leaves and paired flowers that fade from white to yellow. Birds carry the seeds in its red fruits. Its early spring leaves and long autumn growing season help it form dense shade beneath woodland edges and trees. Across invaded parts of eastern North America, that thick understory can crowd out native plants.

lernaea-cyprinacea.summary: Anchor worm is a tiny crustacean related to other copepods. After mating, the female embeds an anchor-shaped front end in a freshwater fish, leaving her elongated body and egg sacs outside. Carp and goldfish are frequent hosts, though many other fish can be affected. Attachment wounds and damage to gills make heavy infestations a concern, especially in warm, slow-moving water.

eichhornia-azurea.summary: Anchored water hyacinth is an aquatic perennial whose roots usually remain fixed in mud while its stems and leaves spread across the water. Showy blue-purple flowers rise above the leaves, and the leaf stalks lack the inflated floats familiar from common water hyacinth. It grows in warm, slow-moving rivers, lakes, and marshes. Its dense mats change aquatic habitat, although research on its impacts remains limited.

sources.label: USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species: Anchored waterhyacinth

brugmansia-suaveolens.summary: Angel's tears is a woody South American plant known for its large, hanging trumpet flowers. Their evening fragrance attracts moths, linking the plant's daily rhythm to its nighttime pollinators. It is widely recognizable in cultivation, yet Cambridge University Botanic Garden describes the species as extinct in its native wild habitat. This poisonous ornamental has a very different conservation story from many familiar garden escapes.

sources.label: Cambridge University Botanic Garden: Angel's trumpet
Cambridge University Botanic Garden: Brugmansia suaveolens

opuntia-microdasys.summary: Angel's-wings, also called bunny ears cactus, forms branching clumps of flattened green pads dotted with tiny bristles. Those dots are clusters of barbed glochids that detach readily, even though the plant lacks the long spines of many cacti. Creamy-yellow flowers may be followed by reddish-purple fruits. Detached pads can root, helping explain how a small ornamental can expand into a spreading patch in suitable dry conditions.

dichanthium-aristatum.summary: Angleton bluestem is a perennial pasture grass with slender stems and a seed head made of several narrow branches. A patch of dense hairs just below the lowest branch is a useful identification clue. It tolerates seasonal flooding and waterlogged clay soils, and spreads by seed and creeping stems. Its ability to persist under heavy grazing can let it dominate less grazing-tolerant vegetation.

sitotroga-cerealella.summary: The Angoumois grain moth is a small, pale gray-brown moth whose caterpillars spend their development hidden inside grain kernels. Wheat, corn, rice, and other cereals can contain feeding damage before much is visible outside. Adults do not eat the grain, and infestations lack the conspicuous webbing made by some other storage moths. Hollowed kernels and nearby flying adults offer clues to its presence.

sources.label: Canadian Grain Commission: Angoumois grain moth

cowpea-mild-mottle-virus.summary: Cowpea mild mottle virus infects cowpea and several other crop and wild hosts. Leaves may develop pale patches, mottling, curling, or distortion, although the symptoms can be subtle. Whiteflies transmit the virus, and seed transmission has been reported in some hosts. Because similar-looking leaf symptoms have many possible causes, the crop name or appearance alone cannot establish which virus is present.

sources.label: EFSA PERSEUS pest survey review via IPPC: Cowpea mild mottle virus

avena-sterilis.summary: Animated oat is an annual wild oat of crop fields, roadsides, and disturbed ground. Its large florets usually fall in pairs and carry long, bent, twisting awns, useful clues when comparing it with common wild oat. It can travel as a contaminant of cereal seed and grain. A life cycle closely matching annual crops helps it persist in fields and makes separation at harvest difficult.

sources.label: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Avena sterilis identification

myrrhis-odorata.summary: Sweet cicely is a perennial herb with finely divided, fernlike leaves and an anise-like scent. Pale green foliage appears early in spring, followed by umbrella-shaped clusters of small flowers. Native from the Pyrenees toward the Caucasus, it has a long history in gardens. The scientific name is useful here because the common name anise can point to quite different plants.

sources.label: Dutch Association of Botanical Gardens: Sweet cicely

rapistrum-rugosum.summary: Annual bastardcabbage starts with a broad rosette of lobed leaves, then sends up branched stems carrying small yellow flowers. Its two-part, beaked fruits are a better identification clue than the flowers alone. It grows readily in roadsides, fields, and other disturbed places. In invaded Texas habitats, its large basal leaves and dense stands can leave little growing space for nearby native plants.

poa-annua.summary: Annual bluegrass is a small grass familiar in lawns, gardens, and golf courses. Look for pale green growth, boat-shaped leaf tips, and seed heads that can form even under close mowing. It grows best during cooler weather and can produce seed quickly. Some populations behave as perennials, so the everyday name does not capture the full range of its life cycle.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Annual bluegrass

phalaris-canariensis.summary: Annual canarygrass carries compact, egg-shaped to cylindrical flower heads above flat leaves. Close inspection reveals broad, winged coverings around the individual spikelets, giving the head a distinctive overlapping texture. This annual grass grows from fibrous roots and occurs along roadsides and in disturbed ground. Its short, dense heads are useful features to check before confusing it with taller, spreading perennial canary grasses.

sources.label: University of British Columbia: E-Flora BC canarygrass

iberis-amara.summary: Annual candytuft is a small, upright mustard-family plant grown for clusters of lightly fragrant flowers. Each flower has four petals, with the outer pair larger, and the flowering cluster stretches as the fruits develop. It occurs beyond gardens in old fields, lawns, and disturbed ground. Those uneven petals and rounded, notched fruits help separate it from the many other small mustards found in similar places.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Iberis amara

vulpia-myuros.summary: Annual fescue, often called rattail fescue, has fine, folded leaves and long, narrow flower heads tipped with slender bristles. It completes its life cycle as an annual and can blend into a mixed stand of grasses until the heads develop. Some references call it Festuca myuros. That alternate name is worth recognizing when comparing botanical guides or local records of this grass.

stachys-annua.summary: Annual hedgenettle is a small member of the mint family with toothed leaves and pale yellow to white flowers. It grows from a taproot and completes its life in one season, unlike hedgenettles that spread by underground rhizomes. Fields, roadsides, and waste ground are typical places to encounter it. Flower color and the narrowing leaf bases help distinguish it from the similar field hedgenettle.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Stachys annua

mercurialis-annua.summary: Annual mercury is a branching herb with small, inconspicuous flowers and toothed, pointed leaves. Male flowers appear in longer clusters, while female flowers sit singly or in small groups; plants are usually separate sexes, although other arrangements occur. It occupies open, disturbed habitats. Its varied breeding systems have made this otherwise easily overlooked weed an interesting subject for research on plant reproduction.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Mercurialis annua
USDA APHIS: Mercurialis annua weed risk assessment
Hesse and Pannell: Sexual dimorphism in Mercurialis annua

polypogon-monspeliensis.summary: Annual rabbitsfoot grass earns its name from soft, densely packed flower heads that turn from pale green toward tan. It forms clumps in moist ground, including ditch banks, stream edges, pastures, and irrigated fields. Mild winters allow it to grow as a winter annual, while colder places favor summer growth. It reproduces by seed, and its fluffy heads are the clearest feature to notice.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Rabbitfoot polypogon

lolium-multiflorum.summary: Annual ryegrass grows vigorously through cool weather and is familiar as a forage, turf, and cover-crop grass. It also turns up in agricultural land and other disturbed places, where its rapid growth can make it weedy. Plants may survive for more than one season. Crosses with perennial ryegrass can blur the usual identification features, so the boundary between the two is not always obvious in the field.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Italian ryegrass

diplotaxis-muralis.summary: Annual wallrocket is a low, yellow-flowered mustard with most of its toothed or lobed leaves near the base. Slender flowering stems eventually bear narrow seed pods. It often grows beside roads and in dry, disturbed ground, and some plants survive beyond a single year. Compared with perennial wallrocket, it generally has fewer leaves up the stem, a useful detail when the two look similar.

sources.label: University of Udine Flora: Diplotaxis muralis

melilotus-indicus.summary: Annual yellow sweetclover is a small, branching legume with three-part leaves and short clusters of tiny yellow flowers. Its nearly round pods usually contain a single seed and show a fine network of surface veins. It occurs in cultivated and disturbed ground, including orchards and winter cereal fields. The small flowers and compact pods are helpful details when distinguishing it from other sweetclovers.

tapinoma-litorale.summary: Tapinoma litorale nests in hollow twigs and vines, using small plant cavities that can easily escape notice during a casual walk. A survey of Florida Keys ants documented it on numerous islands, from Key Largo to Key West. The researchers treated it as native to Florida and the West Indies, placing this inconspicuous ant within the region's resident tropical fauna.

sources.label: Journal of Insect Science: Ants of the Florida Keys

anoecia-vagans.summary: This aphid links dogwood shrubs with the hidden world beneath grass. Its seasonal cycle moves between Cornus sanguinea and grass roots, including those of cereals; the root-feeding adults range from pale yellow to olive. Spring migrants differ from the similar dogwood aphid Anoecia corni in lacking its dark rear abdominal patch, a useful distinction when investigating aphids around dogwoods and nearby turf.

aphis-eugeniae.summary: Aphis eugeniae is associated with tropical and subtropical plants, with spurges and Glochidion among its important hosts. The specialist identification guide records it from eastern and southeastern Asia and Australia, and notes that it can share a host with Aphis spiraecola in Hawaii. That overlap makes the plant alone an unreliable identification clue; the guide does not implicate this species in plant-virus transmission.

asiphonella-dactylonii.summary: Much of this aphid's life takes place near or below the soil surface on grasses such as bermudagrass. The small root-feeding forms are pale yellow-green with a darker head and a bluish wax coating. In China its life cycle includes Chinese pistache, while populations elsewhere can persist on grass roots without a sexual generation, helping explain why it may be encountered far from its woody host.

cerataphis-lataniae.summary: A flattened brown body edged with white wax gives this palm aphid an appearance quite unlike the familiar green garden aphid. It occurs on palms in tropical settings and glasshouses, including fan palms and raffia palms. Older records need care because it has often been confused with Cerataphis brasiliensis; microscopic hairs beneath the head help separate them, so damage attributed to one should not automatically be assigned to the other.

dysaphis-crataegi.summary: The hawthorn-carrot aphid can be easy to miss because colonies occupy the carrot crown and roots, often just below the soil surface. Individuals vary from yellowish gray to greenish gray and carry a light wax coating. Ants around the plant base can provide a clue to these concealed colonies, making a look at the crown more informative than inspecting only the exposed foliage.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Crown and root aphids

eucallipterus-tiliae.summary: Sticky pavement beneath a linden can reveal this aphid before the insects themselves are noticed. Colonies feed beneath the leaves and release abundant honeydew, which can also support dark sooty mold on surfaces below. Established trees usually tolerate feeding, although saplings can lose normal growth; the aphids remain associated with lindens through their seasonal cycle rather than switching to another kind of plant.

geoica-setulosa.summary: Geoica setulosa lives on grass roots, where its relationship with ants can make it more noticeable than its underground feeding. USDA researchers documented colonies associated with mound-building ants in turf; the mounds themselves disrupted mowing. Its host list includes numerous grasses, so finding it beneath a lawn does not point to a single grass species, and its presence should be distinguished from the visible effects of its ant partners.

sources.label: USDA Agricultural Research Service: Geoica setulosa in eastern North America

geopemphigus-floccosus.summary: Tufts of white wax cover the pale body of this small root aphid. It has been collected on morning-glory roots and recorded across parts of the Americas, including the southern United States. Its underground habits contrast with the conspicuous galls made by many related aphids: a proposed connection to galls on Mexican pistache remains unconfirmed, so that possible alternate host should not be treated as established biology.

greenidea-ficicola.summary: This fig-feeding aphid has a pear-shaped body and strikingly long, outward-curving cornicles, the paired tubes near its rear. Colonies occur on young fig leaves, shoots and sometimes fruit, including ornamental Ficus plants that have helped carry it beyond its original range. Colors vary from green to brown, while the unusually long cornicles offer a more useful clue than color alone.

hyalopterus-amygdali.summary: A coating of white wax gives this slender green aphid its mealy appearance on the undersides of almond leaves. It also occurs on apricot and migrates to reeds, connecting orchard trees with wetland vegetation over its seasonal cycle. Closely related Hyalopterus species look very similar, and reed populations are not all securely distinguished, so records based only on a pale, powdery colony need careful interpretation.

hyperomyzus-lactucae.summary: Sowthistles provide an important home for this broad-bodied green aphid, whose colonies favor young leaf undersides. In seasonal climates its cycle also involves currants or gooseberries, while mild Hawaiian conditions allow successive generations of females throughout the year. Its agricultural importance extends beyond plants where it forms colonies: visiting winged aphids can transmit viruses even to crops on which they cannot complete development.

hyperomyzus-picridis.summary: On a hawkweed oxtongue, a small colony just below the flower heads may belong to Hyperomyzus picridis. Wingless adults are glossy yellow-green with dusky cornicles and brownish markings between body segments. The seasonal cycle links alpine currant with herbs such as Picris and Crepis; this specific host pairing helps explain where to look, without assuming that every green aphid on a daisy-family plant is the same species.

macrosiphoniella-tanacetaria.summary: Summer tansy flowers can carry this relatively large aphid, often more than three millimeters long. Its gray-green body has a light wax covering, contrasting with dark legs, antennae and rear tubes. Colonies gather around flowering stems and flower heads, and the seasonal cycle stays on tansy, making the plant a useful place to observe successive generations.

macrosiphum-lilii.summary: A purple blotch on a pale yellow or orange abdomen gives the purplespotted lily aphid its memorable name. Long black antennae and cornicles, along with dark knees and feet, add to its distinctive appearance on Asiatic lilies. Like other sap-feeding aphids it releases sugary honeydew, so shiny deposits on leaves can draw attention to a colony before its unusual markings are noticed.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Purplespotted lily aphid

melanaphis-sorini.summary: This tiny Miscanthus aphid ranges from tan to wine-purple. Recorded in Japan and Taiwan, it has also been introduced to California and Florida. Its resemblance to a sugarcane-associated relative can be misleading: a studied Florida population did not establish on sugarcane, making the host especially important when interpreting a report or examining an ornamental grass colony.

metopolophium-festucae.summary: This grass-feeding aphid may be green, yellow-green or salmon pink, with dark abdominal bands in the winged form. Its name encompasses populations that differ subtly in their relationship with cereals. The typical form mainly inhabits wild grasses, while the separately named subspecies cerealium is more closely associated with grain crops; that distinction matters when interpreting agricultural records filed under the broader species name.

metopolophium-festucae-cerealium.summary: The cereal-associated form of Metopolophium festucae feeds on crops including wheat, barley and oats. Wingless adults are pale yellow and elongated, while winged adults carry darker markings across the back. Significant infestations documented in the Pacific Northwest drew attention to this subspecies, but an occurrence does not by itself establish crop loss: numbers, crop stage and the activity of aphid predators all influence its practical importance.

sources.label: Kansas State University: Metopolophium festucae cerealium

myzaphis-rosarum.summary: Small rose aphids can remain hidden inside rose leaflets that have not yet unfolded. Myzaphis rosarum is a tiny yellow-green to green species with short antennae and swollen cornicles, feeding along veins on both sides of leaves. It also uses shrubby cinquefoils, and outbreaks are uncommon; its discreet habits make it easy to overlook among the more conspicuous aphids found on garden roses.

myzus-varians.summary: Tightly rolled, cigar-shaped peach leaves are a characteristic sign of this aphid's feeding. Pale green wingless adults gather beneath the leaves, whose margins curl lengthwise and may redden as the damage develops. The seasonal cycle includes eggs near peach buds and a migration to clematis, showing how an insect noticed in an orchard can depend on a quite different plant later in the year.

pleotrichophorus-chrysanthemi.summary: Florists' chrysanthemums host this pale green to yellowish aphid, which can gather in large colonies beneath yellowing leaves. Adults are roughly two millimeters long, and no sexual forms are known in the specialist account. Its close resemblance to Pleotrichophorus glandulosus has raised questions about their separation, so careful identification is useful when tracing greenhouse infestations or comparing records made under the two names.

rhopalomyzus-lonicerae.summary: This aphid changes both host and appearance through the season. Spring colonies on honeysuckle contain dark green, wax-dusted insects that roll leaves downward and produce yellow or red spotting. Later generations move to grasses, especially reed canarygrass, where pale yellow colonies develop on the leaves; recognizing that connection helps make sense of two very different-looking infestations near the same patch of vegetation.

rhopalosiphum-rufiabdominalis.summary: The rice root aphid spends much of its life out of sight on underground plant parts. Despite its common name, it uses many grasses, sedges and some broadleaf crops; populations can also persist in warm greenhouses and hydroponic systems. Root-feeding adults range from green to brown with rusty coloring toward the rear, and the accepted spelling Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale frequently appears in specialist literature.

sipha-glyceriae.summary: Wetland grasses are a good place to encounter Sipha glyceriae, a small green aphid that sometimes has reddish coloring or a paler stripe along its back. Its recorded plants include sweetgrasses and other grasses as well as sedges and rushes. It completes its seasonal cycle without a woody alternate host, linking its biology directly to the herbaceous vegetation of marshy places.
